Josias Simler
yō-sē'as zim'ler
n. (Josias Simler, 1530–1576, Zurich professor of theology and biographer of the Reformers)
Hebrew Yoshiyahu, the LORD supports, through Josias; Simler, a Swiss family name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Josias Simler was the son of a Zurich pastor, brought up partly in Bullinger's house, and from 1560 professor of theology in the Zurich school, where he lectured on the Old Testament and wrote commentaries on Exodus and the Gospels. His lasting service was of another kind. He wrote the lives of the men he had known — Peter Martyr Vermigli, Heinrich Bullinger, the naturalist Conrad Gesner, his own father-in-law — promptly, carefully, and from the papers and the testimony of those still living, and most of what later ages know of the second Zurich generation rests on his work. He also edited Vermigli's Loci Communes, which carried Reformed theology across Europe in a usable form. He was dead at forty-six of the gout that had crippled him for years. The church owes him the unglamorous debt it owes every faithful recorder: without him the Zurich Reformation would be a set of conclusions without faces. “by it he being dead yet speaketh” (Heb 11:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines biography as the history of the life and character of a particular person, and memory as the remembrance of a person or thing.

BIOG'RAPHY, n. The history of the life and character of a particular person.

MEM'ORY, n. The faculty of the mind by which it retains knowledge; remembrance; the reputation of one deceased.

COM'MONPLACES, n. In theology, the chief heads or topics of doctrine, treated in order.

RECORD'ER, n. One whose official duty is to register writings or transactions.

Key Scripture

Heb 11:4 — "By faith Abel offered unto God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, by which he obtained witness that he was righteous, God testifying of his gifts: and by it he being dead yet speaketh."

Pro 10:7 — "The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot."

Psa 112:6 — "Surely he shall not be moved for ever: the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance."

Modern Corruption

The Zurich professor who wrote down the lives of the men he had known.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern suspicion of the memorial life as a genre: because Simler admired his subjects, his lives are discounted as hagiography. He was writing within a few years of the deaths, for readers who had known the men, and his biographies can be checked against the surviving correspondence; where they have been, they stand up.

The principle to recover is that remembering the faithful is commanded and useful, and that the use is imitation rather than sentiment: “That ye be not slothful, but followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises” (Heb 6:12). Solomon states the plain contrast that makes such recording worth a lifetime: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot” (Pro 10:7).
